chapter: Earl King, later career and gear
title: Arranging in the 1960s and playing around New Orleans now
summary: Arranging, being a sideman, Continental brunch gig, Preservation Hall, Bourbon Street, retirement.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: So in the 60s how much more arranging did you do like for recordings, etcetera?
Well I did, I ran for quite a few people, you know. I don't get much, it looked like.
Much recording and work. Yeah. Yeah.

I'm doing some things for myself, I'm trying to get recorded, man. You know, I just haven't had the money to do nothing. But I've been writing on some things, you know. I played on a lot of other guys' stuff, but I never really did nothing for myself yet, you know, featuring myself, you know.
Well you think you've always been known as a side man. Yeah. I've always known Curtis Mitchell as a solid side man, you know. But never the front man, never the front guy.
Nah. Nah. Well see I play out there in the Continental every Sunday morning.
Yeah, brunch every Sunday morning. I've been playing there for about eight, nine years now, with Greg, Greg Stafford. Yeah. Me and Greg, Michael White, and Steve Bailock on guitar.
And I do a lot of singing around there.
You know where before I wasn't singing, you know, since I started singing I said, well, I'm going to try to record something for me too.
When did you start, like really, was it the 60s when you got off the road and you started just doing gigs in New Orleans? Yeah. Doing mostly gigs in New Orleans. Yeah, right. Yeah.
So have you been doing mostly, what do you call it traditional?
Traditional, yeah. Most traditional, yeah. I've been getting most gigs now on bass.

And lately I've been getting a few gigs at the Preservation Hall, some on bass, and some on piano. You know I played last week on piano down there. At the hall? Yeah, Preservation Hall. And then they called me a few times to play bass too. But I played in almost every club down there on Bourbon Street. The Paddock Lounge and everywhere down there, man. As a matter of fact I don't really like to play on Bourbon Street no more because the hours are so long and sometimes I get a job paying two or three hours and make it more than I'm playing for five hours down there, man. You know? Yeah. Yeah. And then I'm drawing my Social Security. Then I get a check from the union too. You know, so. I'm really, I've really been waiting on this because I can practice when I want it. I ain't got to worry about paying a rent, you know? Yeah.
